Forecasters attempting to predict infectious disease outbreaks have met with varying success.
This variation may be attributed to varying predictive power between forecast estimation methods, or to varying difficulty between forecast target estimands.
Attributing performance is especially challenging when faced with many forecasters estimating many different forecast target estimands.
In this case, using aggregated summary statistics may obscure different sources of variation underlying individual forecast performance.
Here, we developed a regression framework to identify partial effects on forecast performance, adjusting for factors contributing to forecast target difficulty.

We evaluated forecasts of incident COVID-19 cases and deaths over two years for 32 European countries. We evaluated forecasts against observed data using the Weighted Interval Score (WIS).
We classified 47 forecasting models by structure (agent-based, mechanistic, semi-mechanistic, statistical, or human judgement), estimating the partial effect on performance. We used a generalised additive mixed model to adjust for the target epidemiological outcome, burden, trend, dominant variant phase; country location, forecast horizon, and individual model variation.

After adjustment for features of the forecast target, no single structural approach dominated.
Our findings suggest that variation in European Covid-19 forecast performance is driven more by differences among features of the forecast target, than by differences among specific modelling approaches.

This method of analysis represents a middle ground in formally considering bias when designing evaluation studies.
As the field of infectious disease forecasting expands, we encourage evaluators to consider a wider range of study designs, adopting informal to formal methods where appropriate in order to isolate specific components of forecast performance.
